paras: The threatened lynching on Union Street, Bellaire, was an incident late on the evening of Monday, May 30, 1881, in which a crowd of men from Wheeling was reported to be preparing to lynch a Bellaire, Ohio, resident on Union street. Help arrived before the crowd acted, and the only report said no serious damage was done. The episode is known from a single line in the Wheeling Register's Bellaire column, which named no one and gave neither a cause nor the man's race.
At the time Bellaire was holding a Loan Exhibition, which drew large crowds and filled most of the Register's Bellaire column of June 1 with notes on its contests and visiting delegations.

According to the Register's Bellaire correspondent, "a crowd of wheeling roughs were preparing to lynch one of our citizens on Union street late Monday evening, when aid arrived and no serious damage was done." The item does not say who the man was, what the crowd held against him, how large it was, or who came to his aid.
No report of arrests, charges or any later proceedings in the matter was found in the coverage.

The Wheeling Register ran the item without a headline among routine Bellaire notes, between a report of a beer wagon tipping over on Gravel Hill and a call to attend a meeting on the county seat question. Its wording cast the attackers as outsiders, "wheeling roughs," and the target as "one of our citizens," and it used no racial terms. No other paper's account of the incident was found.
